titulo: Modals of Obligation, Permission and Ability
descripcion: At A2 you use have to for obligation, can for ability and permission, and can't for prohibition. These are the three most useful modal meanings at this level. These forms are the building blocks for more nuanced modal use at higher levels.

ejemplos.texto: I have to work early tomorrow.
Can I open the window, please?

notas: Have to changes with the subject: I have to, she has to.
Can is used for both permission and ability.
Can't expresses either prohibition or inability, depending on context.

contraste.es: Spanish has tener que and poder as close equivalents, so the logic transfers easily.
contraste.de: Can and können match well, and can't corresponds to nicht dürfen (Du darfst hier nicht rauchen – You can't smoke here). Have to corresponds to müssen; careful with must not, which means nicht dürfen, not nicht müssen.
contraste.it: Potere corresponds to can, and non si può to you can't (qui non si può fumare – you can't smoke here). Dovere covers both must and have to; at A2, have to is the safer everyday choice.
contraste.fr: Pouvoir corresponds to can, and on ne peut pas to you can't (on ne peut pas fumer ici – you can't smoke here). Devoir covers must and have to; at A2, have to is the safer everyday choice.
contraste.pt: Ter de or ter que corresponds exactly to have to, and poder to can (aqui não se pode fumar – you can't smoke here). The three A2 modals therefore transfer very well.

errores: Forgetting has for she/he/it with have to.
Using must instead of can for permission.
autochequeo: Is can used for permission and ability correctly?
Have I used at least three different modals?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on have to, can and can't. Check the form has for third person. Do not rewrite the text. Flag anything unclear. Check whether the sentence sounds natural, not translated from Spanish.

es: *tengo que ir* rendered as *I have that go* instead of *I have to go*.
de: Using *must* for the past, since *musste* looks like it: *Yesterday I must work* instead of *Yesterday I had to work*.
it: *so guidare* rendered with *know*: *I know drive* instead of *I can drive*.
fr: *je sais conduire* rendered with *know*: *I know drive* instead of *I can drive*.
pt: *tenho que ir* rendered as *I have that go* instead of *I have to go*.
